Entity: Irrigation-precipitation recycling / SGMA
Fact: AN INFLOW TERM MY C6 MODEL DOES NOT CONTAIN: CALIFORNIA IRRIGATION MAY BE PARTLY FEEDING THE COLORADO. Lo & Famiglietti 2013 (Geophys. Res. Lett.) find that Central Valley irrigation initiates an anthropogenic loop in the regional hydrological cycle — summer precipitation +15%, with a corresponding increase in COLORADO RIVER STREAMFLOW of ~30%. Famiglietti's own framing: 'If we stop irrigating in the Valley, we'll see a decrease in stream flow in the Colorado River basin.' Meanwhile California's SGMA requires critically-overdrafted basins to reach groundwater sustainability by 2040 (others 2042), with 500,000 to 1,000,000 acres of San Joaquin Valley farmland projected to be fallowed, retired or repurposed by 2040.
Source: Lo & Famiglietti 2013, GRL doi:10.1002/grl.50108 (open copy: escholarship.org/uc/item/2887w41x); UC Irvine release 2013-01-28; PPIC + Water Education Foundation on SGMA acreage
Notes: ADOPTED AS A STRUCTURAL MECHANISM, NOT A LIVE DRIVER — three caveats the source framing omits. (1) MODEL, NOT OBSERVATION: this is a single coarse-resolution GCM study with PARAMETERIZED convection, and the subsequent literature finds that parameterized-convection schemes MAY OVERESTIMATE REMOTE PRECIPITATION RESPONSES relative to convection-permitting simulations — so ~30% should be read as a plausible UPPER BOUND, not a central estimate. (2) TIMELINE MISMATCH, and it is decisive: SGMA sustainability lands in 2040; the Colorado cuts are 2027-2028. THE FEEDBACK CANNOT BE DRIVING THE CURRENT CUTS, and any framing that implies it does is wrong on the clock. (3) WHY IT STILL MATTERS: it is an INDEPENDENT antecedent — anthropogenic land use, NOT ENSO — so it does not double-count against my ENSO root, and it points the SAME direction as the Upper-Basin dipole-pivot guard (KB-054). My inflow model has terms for snowpack and ENSO and NO term for anthropogenic precipitation recycling. Under my own C6 discriminator this graduates past 'watch-note' because SGMA has reached an ACREAGE decision (500k-1M acres).

Entity: Ogallala irrigation -> downwind July precipitation -> Mississippi
Fact: A STRUCTURAL HEADWIND ON C5 THAT MY RIVER MODEL DOES NOT CONTAIN. DeAngelis et al. 2010 (J. Geophys. Res. Atmospheres) find 20th-century July precipitation increased 15-30% in a broad region downwind of the Ogallala Aquifer, from eastern Kansas through Indiana, with the timing (post-WWII), the month (July) and the spatial pattern consistent with the history of Ogallala irrigation. A 2015 J. Hydrometeorology study reports observational evidence that Great Plains irrigation enhanced summer precipitation intensity and totals in the Midwest. The Ogallala is fossil water that cannot meaningfully recharge on civilizational timescales, so this precipitation subsidy is finite.
Source: DeAngelis et al. 2010, JGR-Atmos doi:10.1029/2010JD013892; J. Hydrometeorology 16(4) 2015 doi:10.1175/JHM-D-14-0115.1

CAVEATS, held firmly: (a) same model/attribution caution as KB-061 — these are attribution studies over a century of station data, not a forecast; (b) I have NOT quantified how much of Mississippi flow this represents and will not assert one; (c) the decline is DECADAL, so this is a Tier-2 structural note with the horizon stated, NOT a C5 score-mover.
